title: Cocharacter parabolics, split radicals and projective homogeneous quotients
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $G$ be a reductive $k$-group [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology, def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]: it is smooth, affine, geometrically connected and of finite type, and over an algebraic closure has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Smoothness, connectedness, and finite type are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. A smooth affine group is unipotent if its geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful finite-dimensional representation. Let $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\to G$ be a homomorphism [def-sc-gm-ga]. For every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, define $P_\lambda(A)$ to consist of $g\in G(A)$ for which $t\mapsto\lambda(t)g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ extends to a morphism $\mathbf A^1_A\to G_A$; here $\mathbf A^1_A=\operatorname{Spec}A[t]$. Define $U_\lambda(A)$ by requiring this extension to have value $1$ at zero. Define $Z_\lambda(A)$ by requiring $g$ to commute with $\lambda(s)$ after every $A$-algebra extension and for every unit $s$. These functors are represented by smooth geometrically connected closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], $U_\lambda$ is normal in $P_\lambda$, and evaluation at zero is a retraction $r_\lambda:P_\lambda\to Z_\lambda$ with kernel $U_\lambda$. Multiplication gives an isomorphism $U_\lambda\rtimes Z_\lambda\simeq P_\lambda$, with product $(u,z)(v,w)=(uzvz^{-1},zw)$. The group $U_\lambda$ is split unipotent: it admits a finite series of smooth connected closed subgroups, each normal in its predecessor, with quotients $\mathbf G_a$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. The quotient sheaf $G/P_\lambda$, namely fppf sheafification of $A\mapsto G(A)/P_\lambda(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings, is represented by a smooth projective geometrically integral $k$-scheme $X_\lambda$. Projective means admitting a closed immersion into some projective space [def-pc-projective-morphism]; geometrically integral means nonempty, reduced and irreducible after every field extension. The projection $G\to X_\lambda$ is a smooth surjective right $P_\lambda$-torsor of finite presentation: $(g,p)\mapsto(g,gp)$ is an isomorphism $G\times_kP_\lambda\simeq G\times_{X_\lambda}G$, and its geometric fibres are integral. The scheme $G$ is geometrically integral. Formation of $P_\lambda,U_\lambda,Z_\lambda,r_\lambda$ and $X_\lambda$ commutes with every field extension $L/k$ [def-pc-field-extension, def-pc-fibre-product]. Finally, let $T\subseteq G$ be a split maximal torus [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type] and suppose $\lambda$ factors through $T$. If $\alpha\circ\lambda(t)=t^{n_\alpha}$ has $n_\alpha\ne0$ for every nontrivial $T$-character $\alpha$ occurring in the conjugation representation on the tangent space $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ at $1$, then $Z_\lambda=T$.

source.place: Milne Theorem 13.33(a)-(e), printed pp.265-266; Proposition 17.60, p.372 (split unipotent kernel); Theorem 25.1, p.544 (parabolic quotient), with Theorems 5.28 and 8.43-8.44, pp.105,161 (represented, quasi-projective quotient, hence projective when proper). Regular centralizer: proof of Proposition 21.29, pp.433-434. Smooth integral geometry: Corollary 5.26, Proposition 7.15 and Propositions 1.34-1.35. The field-extension clauses use the defining functors and quotient sheaf.

proof.text: Construct the limit functors over $k$, before extending the field. For the conjugation action $c$ on the smooth affine scheme $G$, apply [lem-sfb-smooth-affine-concentrator] with invariant smooth closed subscheme $G$, and then with the identity subscheme $e=\operatorname{Spec}k$. These give smooth closed schemes $P$ and $U$ and the universal limit morphism $C:\mathbf A^1\times P\to G$. Products and inverses of extended orbit maps extend the orbit of a product and inverse, so these are closed subgroup schemes. Construct the fixed scheme $Z$ by imposing the coefficients of $c^*(f)-1\otimes f$ for $f\in k[G]$ in $k[t,t^{-1}]\otimes_k k[G]$; its points over every test algebra are precisely the stated universal commuting points. This is a closed subgroup and is smooth by [lem-sfb-torus-fixed-scheme-smooth], applied to $\mathbf G_m$ acting on $G$. All three constructions represent the actual test-algebra functors, including on nonreduced algebras.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(a), pp.265--266; Definition 13.21, Proposition 13.23 and the definition of Z, pp.261--264.

proof.text: The identities $C(s,C(t,g))=C(st,g)$ and $C(t,gh)=C(t,g)C(t,h)$ hold first when $s,t$ are invertible and hence everywhere: on coordinate rings, Laurent restriction $A[s,t]\hookrightarrow A[s^{\pm1},t^{\pm1}]$ is injective for every algebra $A$. Set $t=0$ in the first identity. This says that $r(g)=C(0,g)$ is fixed under conjugation by $\lambda$, so $r:P\to Z$. The second identity makes $r$ a homomorphism. For $z\in Z$, its orbit is constant, so $r(z)=z$. By the definition of $U$, $\ker r=U$; thus $U$ is normal. Multiplication and $g\mapsto(g r(g)^{-1},r(g))$ are mutually inverse morphisms $U\times Z\rightleftarrows P$. Indeed $r(g r(g)^{-1})=1$. Multiplying $uz$ and $vw$ yields $u(zvz^{-1})zw$, giving exactly the displayed semidirect-product group law.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(b) and its proof, p.266; explicit limit and inverse formulas.

proof.text: For any extension $L/k$, an $L$-algebra $A$ has $G_L(A)=G(A)$, and the same orbit map in $G(A[t,t^{-1}])$ extends to $G(A[t])$ in either description. Thus the base changes of $P,U,Z$ represent the three functors for $G_L,\lambda_L$; evaluation at $t=0$ also agrees, giving $r_L$. In particular over an algebraic closure $\bar k$, [lem-sfb-cocharacter-limit-smooth-structure] says these three represented functors are connected. Their representing schemes are the schemes already constructed, by the uniqueness of a representing object. The geometric-connectedness criterion [lem-weil-geometrically-connected-algebraic-closure] now shows that $P,U,Z$ are geometrically connected over $k$. This establishes the connectedness and all subgroup base-extension clauses without assuming $k$ perfect.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(e), pp.265--266; functor definitions of P, U and Z, pp.263--264.

proof.text: Write $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. Use [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] to identify infinitesimal points with $\mathfrak g\otimes_k A$ and conjugation with the algebraic adjoint action. By [lem-sfb-gm-representation-weight-basis], $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_n\mathfrak g_n$ for the action of $\lambda$. For an infinitesimal point represented by $v=\sum_n v_n$, its conjugated tangent vector is $\sum_n t^n v_n$. It extends polynomially across zero exactly when all negative-weight components vanish, and specializes to zero exactly when the weight-zero component also vanishes. Consequently $\operatorname{Lie}(U)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(Z)=\mathfrak g_0$. The first equality has no invariant subspace for the conjugation action of the split torus $\mathbf G_m$. The general action criterion [lem-sfb-split-torus-no-invariants-unipotence], applied to the smooth geometrically connected affine group $U$, therefore supplies its finite $\mathbf G_a$ quotient series over $k$ and its unipotence. This uses integer characters, including in characteristic $p$ when a nonzero weight may be divisible by $p$.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(c), pp.265--266, and proof of Proposition 17.60, p.372.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homogeneous-quotient] to the closed subgroup $P\subset G$ to obtain a separated finite-type quotient $q:G\to X$, flat, surjective and finitely presented. Its equality-of-images criterion identifies its kernel pair with $G\times P$ by $(g,p)\mapsto(g,gp)$; the inverse sends $(g,h)$ to $(g,g^{-1}h)$. These formulas are morphisms on all tests, since the criterion makes $g^{-1}h$ factor through $P$. The map $q$ is itself an fppf covering, and so are its pullbacks by [lem-trf-fppf-covering-base-change]. Thus every test point of $X$ lifts fppf locally to $G$, and the kernel-pair criterion says that any two lifts differ exactly by $P$. This proves that $X$ represents the fppf sheafification of the right-coset functor, with the required right torsor identity. After every $L/k$, the pulled-back covering and the same identity give the same description of $X_L$ as $G_L/P_L$. Uniqueness of sheafification gives the canonical, not just abstract, base-extension isomorphism.

source.place: Theorems 5.28 and Corollary 5.27, p.105; the torsor identity of Lemma 5.24.

proof.text: Pull $q$ back along its fpqc cover $q:G\to X$. Its pullback is the projection $G\times P\to G$, smooth since $P$ is smooth and smoothness is preserved by base change [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2). Hence $q$ is smooth by [lem-trf-smooth-fpqc-base-descent]. Since $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth and $q$ is a flat surjective locally finitely presented map, [lem-sbc-smooth-flat-surjective-source-descent] makes $X$ smooth over $k$. Over every extension field, $G$ is nonempty and connected and maps surjectively to $X$ by [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change], so $X$ is nonempty and connected as a continuous image. Thus $X$ is geometrically connected. Apply [lem-trf-smooth-connected-fibre-normal-integrality] to the structure morphisms of $G$ and $X$: their unique fibres are geometrically connected and their structure morphisms are smooth. It follows that $G$ and $X$ are geometrically integral.

source.place: Corollary 5.26, p.105; Proposition 7.15 and proof, pp.142--143; smooth connected integral geometry.

proof.text:
It remains to prove properness, and then projectivity, of $X$. Work over $F= ar k$. The reductive Borel-pair node supplies a maximal torus $T$ and its root datum; the cocharacter-conjugacy node permits conjugating $\lambda$ into $T$. The conjugation also carries its limit subgroup to the conjugate subgroup, directly from the orbit formula: if $g\lambda g^{-1}=
u$ then $P_
u=gP_{F}g^{-1}$, and right multiplication $x\mapsto xg^{-1}$ on $G_F$ descends to an isomorphism $G_F/P_F\simeq G_F/P_
u$ of the represented coset sheaves. Hence we may and do replace $\lambda$ by $
u$, so that $\lambda$ factors through $T$. Choose an integral cocharacter $\mu$ off all the finitely many root hyperplanes. Such a choice exists in the cocharacter lattice: in a lattice basis evaluate each nonzero integral linear form at $(1,M,\ldots,M^{r-1})$ and avoid its finitely many integer zeros. For $N$ sufficiently large, $\lambda\prime=N\lambda+\mu$ is regular and retains the sign of every nonzero $\langle\alpha,\lambdaangle$. Therefore $\langle\alpha,\lambda\primeangle>0$ implies $\langle\alpha,\lambdaangle\geq0$. In rank zero the root set is empty and take $\lambda\prime=0$. By [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description], $B=P_{\lambda\prime}$ is a Borel containing $T$, with positive roots exactly those with positive $\lambda\prime$-pairing.

source.place: Theorem 25.1, first paragraph of proof, p.544; Proposition 21.29, pp.433--434.

proof.text: For every positive root $\alpha$ of $B$, [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations] gives $\lambda(t)u_\alpha(a)\lambda(t)^{-1}=u_\alpha(t^{n_\alpha}a)$. Here $n_\alpha\geq0$ by the preceding step, so this formula extends to $\mathbf A^1$ over every test algebra; hence $U_\alpha\subset P$. Also $T\subset P$, since it commutes with $\lambda$. The Borel-pair node writes $B=R_u(B)\rtimes T$, and [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates] writes every test-algebra point of $R_u(B)$ as the product of its positive root-group coordinates. Products of the displayed extensions show that the entire inclusion $B\to G$ factors through $P$, scheme-theoretically. The nested quotient node gives a surjection $G_F/B\to G_F/P_F=X_F$. Its source is proper by [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry], and the target is separated and finite type. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-image-universally-closed] makes $X_F$ proper. Finally [lem-pc-proper-descends-field] descends properness to $X/k$.

source.place: Theorem 25.1, p.544; Theorem 17.16 and Proposition 7.15; Stacks Tag 03GN, label lemma-image-proper-is-proper, and Tag 02L1, label lemma-descending-property-proper.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-affine-homogeneous-quotient-projective-immersion] with the smooth affine $G$ and its closed subgroup $P$ to obtain $j:X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$. Its target is separated and its source is now proper, so [lem-weil-pbc-proper-over-separated] makes $j$ proper. Then [lem-weil-pbc-proper-immersion-closed] makes $j$ a closed immersion. This is exactly the finite-projective-space convention of projectivity in the statement, not just properness or projectivity after scalar extension.

source.place: Theorems 7.18, p.143, and 8.43, p.161; Stacks Tag 01W6, label lemma-image-proper-scheme-closed, and Schemes Tag 01IQ, label lemma-immersion-when-closed.

proof.text: To check the fibre assertion, let $x\in X$, extend $\kappa(x)$ to an algebraic closure $\Omega$, and consider $G_x\times_{\kappa(x)}\Omega$. This is nonempty by surjectivity and is finite type (the quotient is finitely presented). Over $\Omega$ it has a rational point: finite-type schemes over a field are Jacobson and their closed-point residue fields over an algebraically closed field are the field, by the two cited closed-point nodes. A chosen point and the torsor identity identify this geometric fibre with $P_\Omega$. It is connected by geometric connectedness of $P$. The algebraic-closure connectedness criterion therefore says $G_x$ is geometrically connected. Its smoothness is inherited from $q$ by base change. Apply [lem-trf-smooth-connected-fibre-normal-integrality] to $q$: every fibre remains nonempty and integral after every extension of its residue field. In particular its geometric fibres are integral as claimed.

source.place: Corollary 5.27, p.105, and Proposition 7.15, pp.142--143; smooth connected integral geometry.

proof.text: For the last clause, extend to $\bar k$. Maximality of $T_{\bar k}$ follows from [lem-sfb-maximal-torus-field-extension]. The weight decomposition of [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] is $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\ne0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$. The assumed nonzero integer pairings eliminate every nontrivial-character summand from the $\lambda$-weight-zero part. Hence the tangent calculation in step 4 gives $\operatorname{Lie}(Z)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ over $\bar k$. We already have $T\subset Z$, and $Z$ is smooth connected. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation] with ambient group $Z$, the single subgroup $T$, and closed subgroup $K=T$; the tangent-spanning hypothesis is exactly this equality. It gives $Z_{\bar k}=T_{\bar k}$. On the affine coordinate rings, the ideal of $T$ inside $Z$ tensors to zero over the field extension, so it was zero: a nonzero vector over $k$ stays nonzero after extension of a basis. Thus $Z=T$ over $k$, including the empty-root and trivial-group cases.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 21.29, printed p.434; maximal-torus scalar extension of 17.82.
